A crossing guard is a person whose job is to help people — especially children — cross a road safely. They stand at a specific spot on the road, stop the traffic when needed, and signal to people when it is safe to walk across.

Think of them as a human traffic controller, but their only focus is making sure people on foot get across the road without getting hurt.

A crossing guard does not just stand and watch. They actively control traffic and people:

  • They step into the road and hold up a handheld stop sign (a paddle-shaped sign that says "STOP") or raise their hand firmly to signal drivers to stop.
  • Once the vehicles have stopped, they signal to the pedestrians — usually with a wave or a nod — that it is now safe to cross.
  • They sometimes walk across with the people, especially with young children, to make sure everyone reaches the other side.
  • They keep a close watch for drivers who are not slowing down or who might ignore the signal.
  • After everyone has crossed, they step back onto the pavement and allow traffic to move again.

In many countries, crossing guards have legal authority to stop traffic. This means drivers are legally required to obey their stop signal, just as they would obey a traffic light or a police officer directing traffic.

Crossing guards are stationed at pedestrian crossings — the marked areas on the road where people are supposed to walk across (also called crosswalks or zebra crossings). You will most commonly find them:

  • Near schools — this is by far the most common location, because children walk to and from school and need extra protection near roads.
  • At busy intersections where traffic is heavy and crossing is risky, even for adults.
  • In areas with poor visibility, such as roads with bends or obstructions, where drivers may not see pedestrians in time.

Crossing guards do not work all day. Their hours are tied to when pedestrian traffic is highest near their assigned spot:

  • Morning, when children and commuters are heading to school or work.
  • Afternoon, when school ends and children walk back home.
  • Sometimes during lunch break, if students are allowed to leave the school grounds midday.

This means a crossing guard's working day is often split into two or three short blocks of time, not a continuous shift.

Crossing guards are easy to spot:

  • They wear brightly coloured vests — usually orange, yellow, or lime green — with reflective strips that catch the light. This makes them visible to drivers from a distance, even in poor weather or low light.
  • They carry a handheld stop sign, which is a paddle or round sign on a stick. In the United Kingdom, this sign is round and orange, and people often call crossing guards "lollipop men" or "lollipop women" because the sign resembles a giant lollipop.
  • Some crossing guards also wear a uniform, a cap, or a badge that identifies their official role.

Crossing guards can be:

  • Paid workers hired by a school district, a city government, or a local council.
  • Volunteers, such as parents of students or retired community members who take on this role out of goodwill.
  • In some schools, particularly in older traditions, senior students are assigned the role on a rotating basis — they are often called "school patrol" or "safety patrol" members.

Crossing guards are not police officers, but they carry out a small, specific piece of what traffic police do — managing the safe movement of people at a crossing point.

You might wonder: don't traffic lights handle this? Sometimes, yes. But:

  • Not every crossing has a traffic light, especially near schools in quieter neighbourhoods.
  • Children are not always good judges of traffic speed and distance. A crossing guard removes the need for a child to make that judgement call.
  • Drivers pay more attention to a person standing in the road than to painted lines on the ground.
  • Traffic patterns near schools are unpredictable — cars park, buses stop, children run. A human presence helps manage the chaos.

In short, crossing guards exist because some situations are too complex or too risky to be handled by road markings and traffic lights alone. A human being who can assess the situation in real time and react is safer.

A crossing guard is a safety worker stationed at a road crossing — most often near a school — whose job is to stop traffic and help people, especially children, cross the road safely. They wear bright, visible clothing, carry a handheld stop sign, work during peak pedestrian hours, and often have the legal authority to require drivers to stop. They exist because painted crosswalks and traffic lights alone are not always enough to protect people — especially young children — from the dangers of road traffic.
